# Summary

The mortgage delinquency in Canada is closely tied to unemployment. Across 10 provinces, one more percentage point of unemployment goes with about 19% higher delinquency, and a panel of 33 metropolitan areas gives a similar figure (about 17%). Much of this relationship disappears when provinces are compared within the same quarter, so part of it reflects shocks shared across the country. The policy rate effect cannot be identified, because the sample covers a single large cycle. Delinquency changes slowly, so next quarter is hard to predict better than with last quarter’s value: The best model, a random forest fitted to quarterly changes, cuts the error by 8%, but the gain is not statistically significant (p = 0.13).

# Data

The panel covers 10 provinces and 54 quarters, from 2012Q3 to 2025Q4 (540 province-quarters). The CMHC data used here was published in March 2026.

*[Sources: CMHC delinquency, Labour Force Survey unemployment, Bank of Canada policy rate.]*

# Methods

## Why a panel with fixed effects

Provinces differ permanently in ways I cannot observe or measure well, such as housing market structure, lending practices and demographics. Province fixed effects remove these constant differences, so the model compares each province with itself over time: what happens to delinquency in a province when its unemployment changes. This removes omitted variables that are constant within a province, but not those that change over time, which I discuss in the next section. Quarter-of-year effects absorb seasonality. I do not include a full set of date effects, because they would absorb the national policy rate, which only varies over time.

## Omitted variable bias

A fixed effects model adds a dummy variable for each province. These dummies control for any characteristic, observed or not, that is constant within a province over time. They do not control for factors that change over time within a province and move with unemployment, such as local income or house prices. If such factors exist, the unemployment coefficient is biased, and I cannot say in which direction. It as an association, not as a causal effect. The robustness checks show how much of the association is shared across places: in the metropolitan-area models, the coefficient falls from 0.154 to 0.093 when I remove shocks common to all areas in a quarter, and to 0.034 when I compare areas within the same province and quarter. Part of the association reflects common shocks.

## COVID

The COVID period was atypical: payment deferrals and income support likely pushed delinquency down while unemployment spiked, which broke the usual relationship between the two. I set these quarters apart with an indicator for 2020Q2 to 2021Q4. In the main model, the indicator is about -0.50, meaning delinquency was roughly 40% lower in those quarters than unemployment and the policy rate would predict. I also estimate the model without those quarters, and the unemployment coefficient rises from 0.171 to 0.228.


## Inference

I cluster standard errors by province, but 10 clusters is too few to trust them fully, so I treat the intervals as indicative. As a check, I repeat the models on 33 metropolitan areas. The results are similar (0.154 against 0.171), though areas in the same province share shocks, so these standard errors are probably too small.

## Out-of-sample validation

The baseline model is a panel regression with province and quarter-of-year fixed effects, used to measure the association between unemployment, the policy rate and delinquency. To see whether a more flexible model predicts better, I also fit random forests (500 trees, no tuning), which do not assume a functional form and can capture nonlinear effects. 

There is a comparison of all models on quarters they were not fitted on. For each of the 16 test quarters (2022Q1 to 2025Q4), I refit every model on all earlier data and predict one quarter ahead, which gives 160 predictions per model. The reference is a model that only uses last quarter’s delinquency, and I measure error as RMSE in log points. To test whether differences between models are real,  a Diebold-Mariano is performed to test on the average error per quarter. As there are only 16 test quarters the test has low power.

## Scenarios

The scenarios are conditional projections from the persistence plus unemployment model, not forecasts. Starting in 2025Q4, unemployment rises by 0 (baseline), 2 (moderate stress) or 4 (severe stress) percentage points over four quarters and then stays fixed, for a horizon of 8 quarters, with the COVID indicator off. These results are simple averages across provinces, not weighted by number of mortgages, and have no uncertainty bands.


# Results

## Association with unemployment and the policy rate

Unemployment is associated with delinquency in all specifications. In the main model, one more percentage point of unemployment goes with about 19% higher delinquency (coefficient 0.171). The policy rate is negative at every lag, the opposite of the expected sign. It is significant at two quarters (p = 0.009 and 0.029), borderline at four (p = 0.053), and not significant without the COVID quarters (p = 0.144). The figure shows the coefficient by lag: it is negative throughout, and the intervals include zero at lags 4 to 8. With a single rate cycle, it is not possible to split the effect of the policy rate from other things that changed between 2022 and 2025. Also, the delinquency is persistent (last quarter’s delinquency in the model, its coefficient is 0.955, the short-run effect of unemployment falls to 0.011 and the implied long-run effect is 0.245).

```{r}
#| label: fe-table
fe_file <- c("fixed_effects_models.csv", "baseline_models.csv")
fe_file <- fe_file[file.exists(out(fe_file))][1]
rd(fe_file) |>
  mutate(term = recode(term, !!!term_labels),
         cell = sprintf("%.3f (%.3f)", estimate, std.error)) |>
  select(term, model, cell) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = model, values_from = cell) |>
  kable(caption = "Provincial fixed-effects models. Coefficient (standard error).")
```

![](`r fig("rate_lag_profile.png")`)

## Robustness with 33 metropolitan areas

The metropolitan-area results are close to the provincial ones. The unemployment coefficient is 0.154 in the main model (0.171 for provinces) and 0.215 without the COVID quarters (0.228). It falls to 0.093 with date effects (0.148) and to 0.034 when areas are compared within the same province and quarter, where it is only significant at 10% (p = 0.086). With last quarter’s delinquency in the model, persistence is 0.932 and the short-run effect of unemployment is 0.013. The association persists in the city data, but a large part of it is shared across areas at the same time. The standard errors are small because there are many areas and quarters. But the observations are not independent: delinquency changes slowly, and areas in the same province move together. It is important to say that the uncertainty is larger than the standard errors suggest.

```{r}
#| label: cma-table
rd("cma_models.csv") |>
  mutate(term = recode(term, !!!term_labels),
         cell = sprintf("%.3f (%.3f)", estimate, std.error)) |>
  select(term, model, cell) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = model, values_from = cell) |>
  kable(caption = "Metropolitan-area models. Coefficient (standard error).")
```

## Heterogeneity by province

Unemployment is positive in all provinces. In the provincial panel it ranges from 0.09 (Alberta) to 0.30 (Prince Edward Island), and in the metropolitan-area panel from 0.09 (Alberta) to 0.23 (British Columbia). British Columbia in the provincial panel has a lower bound just below zero (-0.001). Each estimate uses about 50 quarters of a highly persistent series, and metropolitan areas within a province are not independent. I therefore treat the intervals as indicative and do not rank provinces.

![](`r fig("heterogeneity.png")`)

## Prediction

Next quarter’s delinquency is mostly predicted by this quarter’s. A model that only uses that already does about as well as the others. Adding unemployment or the policy rate barely improves it: the average error falls from 0.096 to 0.094 and 0.093 log points. The best result comes from a random forest, which cuts the error by 8%. It beats the simple model in 13 of 16 quarters, but with so few quarters the gain cannot be told apart from chance (p = 0.13). Also, the models that leave out last quarter’s delinquency do much worse and all of them underestimated delinquency in the second half of 2023.

```{r}
#| label: validation-table
rd("validation_scores_all.csv") |>
  mutate(model = recode(model, !!!model_labels)) |>
  select(Model = model, MSE = mse, RMSE = rmse, MAE = mae) |>
  kable(digits = 4, caption = "Out-of-sample error, 16 test quarters. Log points.")
```

```{r}
#| label: dm-table
rd("validation_tests.csv") |>
  filter(loss == "mse") |>
  mutate(model = recode(model, !!!model_labels),
         p_value = ifelse(p_value < 0.001, "<0.001", sprintf("%.3f", p_value))) |>
  select(Model = model,
         `Quarters better than baseline (of 16)` = quarters_better,
         `Mean loss difference` = mean_difference,
         `DM statistic` = statistic,
         `p-value` = p_value) |>
  kable(digits = 3,
        caption = "Diebold-Mariano test against the persistence-only baseline (squared error). Positive differences mean lower error than the baseline.")
```

![](`r fig("validation_rmse.png")`)

![](`r fig("validation_actual_vs_predicted.png")`)

## Scenarios

If unemployment rises by 2 points over four quarters, average delinquency after eight quarters is 0.309%, 11.5% above theso 0.278% of the no-change scenario. A 4-point rise gives 0.345%, 24% above. The percentage increase is the same in every province, because the model uses a single unemployment coefficient. In percentage points the increase is largest in Saskatchewan, Manitoba and Newfoundland, which start from the highest delinquency. These are conditional projections, not forecasts, and they carry no uncertainty bands.

```{r}
#| label: scenario-table
rd("scenario_paths.csv") |>
  filter(date == max(date)) |>
  group_by(Scenario = scenario) |>
  summarise(`Average delinquency (%)` = mean(delinquency_rate), .groups = "drop") |>
  kable(digits = 3, caption = "Average delinquency at the end of the 8-quarter horizon.")
```

![](`r fig("scenarios_average.png")`)

![](`r fig("scenarios_by_province.png")`)

# Limitations

*[Association not causation, one rate cycle, 10 provinces, Ontario weight, survey noise, scenarios without intervals.]*
